step_co_sky: Every dot is an aircraft over Europe, captured from the positions they broadcast shortly before this page was last built [D-opensky].
step_co_yesterday: The European network handled the number on screen [[date:network]]. In 2025 it handled 11.1 million flights, and on its busiest day — 18 July 2025 — 37,034: one new flight every 2.3 seconds [S1, D-eurocontrol].
step_co_hero: None of them just took off. Behind each is a choreography of airlines, airports, air traffic controllers and EUROCONTROL’s **Network Manager**. This is the story of one: **FFS101**, a fictional 07:00 Airbus A320neo from Brussels to Rome [S35].
ch_strategic_title: A flight is born on paper
step_st_schedule: FFS101 first exists in an airline network plan, almost a year before it flies: a 07:00 local departure from Brussels for the Summer 2026 season, which runs from the last Sunday of March to the last Saturday of October [S25].
step_st_slots: Brussels Airport has been slot-coordinated since 2003: nobody takes off or lands there without an airport slot from Belgium Slot Coordination ([[BSC]]) [S26]. Rome Fiumicino’s come from Assoclearance [S27]. EU Regulation 95/93 and the [[WASG]] set the rules — including “use it or lose it” at 80% [S21, S22].
step_st_not_ctot: Those two airport slots — one to leave Brussels, one to land in Rome — are not the take-off “slot” a pilot apologises for on board. That one, the [[CTOT]], only appears on the day itself [S7].
step_st_nop: Meanwhile the [[NM]] — EUROCONTROL, with 42 member states — agrees with every air navigation service provider ([[ANSP]]) how much capacity each piece of sky will offer, in the Network Operations Plan ([[NOP]]) [S2, S8, S3].
step_st_forecast: They plan for a lot of traffic. 2025 was back at 2019 levels, and EUROCONTROL’s seven-year forecast keeps climbing [S1, D-eurocontrol].
step_as_patchwork: Europe’s sky is a patchwork: 37 en-route air navigation service providers share 11.5 million km² of continental airspace [S49]. FFS101’s straight line crosses Belgium, Luxembourg, France, Switzerland and Italy.
step_as_rad: Airlines can’t just draw a line. The Route Availability Document ([[RAD]]) says which routes are open when, renewed every 28-day [[AIRAC]] cycle [S17]. Inside Free Route Airspace ([[FRA]]) — about 76 control centres by the end of 2025 — they may fly direct between entry and exit points [S18].
step_as_military: Part of the sky belongs to the military, part of the time: training zones cover about half of Belgian airspace [S28]. Under Flexible Use of Airspace ([[FUA]]) each country publishes tomorrow’s bookings in an Airspace Use Plan ([[AUP]]), which the Network Manager merges for all of Europe [S19].
step_as_pretactical: Six days out, the Network Manager starts comparing forecast demand with expected capacity. On the eve of the flight, at 16:00 UTC in summer, the plan moves into the live system, [[ETFMS]]: tomorrow becomes today [S8].
step_fp_file: The evening before, a dispatcher files FFS101’s flight plan. It may be filed up to 120 hours ahead and, where possible, at least three hours before off-block [S9].
step_fp_ident: Item 7 is the callsign; item 8 says the flight follows instrument rules and is scheduled; items 9 and 10 give the aircraft type and what it can do — radios, navigation, datalink [S9].
step_fp_eobt: Item 13: from Brussels at 05:00 UTC. That is the [[EOBT]], the estimated off-block time — the moment every later deadline counts from [S9, S7].
step_fp_route: Item 15 is the route: cruise speed, flight level and the points in between — here a chain of coordinates joined by direct segments, as [[FRA]] allows [S9, S18].
step_fp_other: Item 18 carries the rest: date of flight, registration and navigation approvals [S9].
step_fp_ifps: It goes to one place: [[IFPS]], the Network Manager’s flight-plan system in Brussels — up to 100,000 messages a day, more than 99% without human hands [S10]. It checks syntax, the route against the RAD and airspace availability, then replies [[ACK]] [S9].
step_fp_distribute: Within seconds the plan reaches every air traffic control unit on the route and the flow-management system. Filing it is also, in effect, a request for a slot [S7, S9].
step_tw_demand: Overnight the flow managers spot trouble: in a Reims sector group on FFS101’s path, more flights want to pass between 05:00 and 07:00 than its controllers can safely handle [S7].
step_tw_regulation: When demand exceeds capacity, the Network Manager and the local Flow Management Position ([[FMP]]) impose a regulation: a place, a time window and an entry rate. Four hours at 28 flights an hour make 112 slots, about two minutes apart [S7].
step_tw_queue: [[CASA]], the slot allocator, queues flights first-planned, first-served by when they would reach the sector. A flight that doesn’t fit is pushed to the next free slot — and the queue grows [S7].
step_tw_sam: FFS101 is in that queue. At 03:00 UTC — two hours before off-block — a Slot Allocation Message ([[SAM]]) arrives: [[CTOT]] 05:42, 27 minutes late [S7].
step_tw_explore: Your turn: drag the sector’s capacity and watch the delay ripple through every flight in the queue. *A simplified model of CASA, not the real algorithm* [S7].
step_de_yesterday: FFS101 is not alone. Flow-management ([[ATFM]]) delay across the network added up to the minutes on screen [[date:network]] [D-eurocontrol].
step_de_causes: Mostly not because of weather: in 2025, ATC capacity and staffing caused 58% of en-route ATFM delay, weather 28% [S1]. The split for that day is on screen [D-eurocontrol].
step_de_year: Across the year the pattern repeats — summer storms and staffing peaks. France accounted for 36% of en-route delay in 2025 [S1, D-eurocontrol].
step_de_report: Every week the Network Manager writes up what happened. This is its latest network situation report, [[live:report]] [D-situation].
step_rr_path: The regulated sector sits right on FFS101’s planned path over north-east France — the country that generated the most en-route delay in 2025 [S1].
step_rr_rrp: At 03:20 the Network Manager offers a Rerouting Proposal ([[RRP]]): east over Germany and Zurich, about 20 NM longer, with a new CTOT of 05:22 [S7]. In 2025 such reroutes saved 277,000 minutes of delay [S3].
step_rr_weigh: The dispatcher weighs 20 fewer minutes of delay against fuel and different route charges. In 2025, hand-picked proposals saved on average 90 NM, 450 kg of fuel and €112 per flight [S3].
step_rr_accept: Accepted. The plan is refiled, and a Slot Revision Message ([[SRM]]) confirms CTOT 05:22 [S7].
step_gr_acdm: Brussels runs Airport Collaborative Decision Making ([[A-CDM]]): the airport, airline, ground handlers, air traffic control and the Network Manager share one timeline of milestones [S13, S14].
step_gr_tobt: Cleaners, caterers, fuel and baggage teams work around the aircraft while passengers board. Handler and airline commit to a Target Off-Block Time — the [[TOBT]] — when it will really be ready [S13].
step_gr_tsat: Air traffic control turns all the TOBTs and slots into a start-up sequence: FFS101 gets a [[TSAT]] of 05:07 so it reaches the runway for its CTOT. The airport keeps the Network Manager updated with [[DPI]] messages [S7, S13].
step_gr_window: The CTOT is part of the clearance: take-off no more than 5 minutes early or 10 minutes late [S7]. Wheels up at 05:24 — inside the window.
step_gr_punctuality: Brussels’ punctuality, day by day [D-eurocontrol]. In 2025 its departure punctuality was just below 2024 [S1].
step_er_skeyes: FFS101 climbs out under skeyes, the Belgian air navigation service provider, which controls the airspace up to [[FL]] 245 — about 7,500 m [S28].
step_er_muac: Above FL245 it belongs to [[MUAC]], EUROCONTROL’s Maastricht centre for the upper airspace of Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and north-west Germany: 1.83 million flights in 2025, more than 16% of Europe’s traffic, about 60% of clearances by datalink ([[CPDLC]]) [S5, S6].
step_er_handovers: Then Germany’s Karlsruhe centre, Zurich, and Italy’s Milano and Roma centres. Each hand-over is agreed computer-to-computer with [[OLDI]] messages before the pilot changes frequency [S43, S30].
step_er_charges: Every country crossed sends a bill. EUROCONTROL’s Central Route Charges Office ([[CRCO]]) charges per zone: distance ÷ 100 × √([[MTOW]]/50) × the zone’s unit rate [S32, S33].
step_er_switzerland: Switzerland charges €167.12 per unit, Italy €73.71 [S34]. On the original route Switzerland is about 18% of the distance but about 32% of the bill. Europe-wide, €11.8 billion of en-route charges were billed in 2025 [S1].
step_ar_descent: Some 200 km out, FFS101 starts down. ENAV’s Roma controllers fit it into Fiumicino’s arrival sequence [S30].
step_ar_onblocks: Landing at 07:04, on blocks at 07:12 — seven minutes after schedule. By the industry’s 15-minute definition that counts as on time, like 76.1% of arrivals in 2025 [S1].
step_ar_fco: Fiumicino averaged 884 flights a day in 2025 and improved its departure punctuality by 10 percentage points [S1]. Its punctuality, day by day [D-eurocontrol].
step_po_analysis: The flight is over; its data life begins. Post-operations analysis compares plan with reality and feeds the lessons into the next season’s plan [S8].
step_po_billing: Delay is attributed to the regulation and its cause, and all-causes delay is collected by [[CODA]] [S36]. The [[CRCO]] bills the route actually flown [S32]. The Performance Review Commission ([[PRC]]) reports on the year [S37].
step_po_matrix: Thirteen kinds of stakeholders touched FFS101 — most of them invisible from seat 14C [S7, S13].
step_po_co2: The climate cost is counted too: gate-to-gate CO₂ in the network reached 216 Mt in 2025 [S1]. On screen, the Data app’s CO₂ and departures indices [D-eurocontrol].
step_po_everyone: More than 30,000 flights a day go through the same choreography [S3]. Here is this year’s traffic for each control provider on FFS101’s path [D-eurocontrol].
gl_NM_def: EUROCONTROL’s role, set by EU law, of designing the European route network and balancing traffic demand against capacity across Europe.
gl_NMOC_def: The Network Manager’s operations room in Brussels, which runs flow management and flight-plan processing for the whole network.
gl_IFPS_exp: Integrated Initial Flight Plan Processing System
gl_IFPS_def: The Network Manager’s single system in Brussels that checks and distributes every IFR flight plan in the IFPS zone — up to 100,000 messages a day.
gl_ANSP_def: An organisation that provides air traffic control for a piece of airspace, such as skeyes in Belgium or ENAV in Italy. Continental Europe has 37 en-route ANSPs.
gl_ACC_def: A control centre that handles aircraft en route, between the airports’ approach zones; an upper area control centre (UAC) handles only high-level traffic.
gl_MUAC_def: EUROCONTROL’s own control centre for the airspace above FL245 over Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and north-west Germany — more than 16% of all European flights pass through it.
gl_FMP_def: The flow-management desk inside each air navigation service provider, which agrees capacity plans and regulations with the Network Manager.
gl_ATFM_def: Managing the flow of flights so that demand never exceeds what controllers can safely handle — mainly by holding flights on the ground with take-off slots.
gl_ATFCM_exp: Air traffic flow and capacity management
gl_ATFCM_def: ATFM plus the planning of capacity itself: from the strategic phase months ahead to the post-operations analysis afterwards.
gl_CASA_def: The Network Manager’s central, largely automatic system that gives regulated flights their take-off slots, first planned, first served.
gl_CTOT_def: The ATFM slot: the take-off time the Network Manager assigns to a regulated flight. The aircraft must take off between 5 minutes before and 10 minutes after it.
gl_SAM_def: The message the Network Manager sends to the airline and the departure airport two hours before off-block, announcing a flight’s CTOT.
gl_SRM_def: A message that moves an already issued CTOT earlier or later.
gl_SLC_def: Tells the airline and ATC that a flight is no longer regulated and its slot is cancelled.
gl_RRP_def: A message from the Network Manager offering a flight a different route — to avoid delay, or to fly shorter or cheaper. The airline accepts by refiling or declines.
gl_REA_def: Tells the Network Manager a regulated flight is ready to go now, so it can try to improve its slot.
gl_DPI_def: Messages an A-CDM airport sends the Network Manager — early, target, actual — so the network knows when a flight will really leave.
gl_A_CDM_def: A shared set of milestones and target times that lets the airport, airlines, ground handlers, ATC and the Network Manager work from the same timeline. About 34 European airports have it fully.
gl_EOBT_def: When the flight plan says the aircraft will push back from the gate — the reference point for most other deadlines.
gl_TOBT_def: The airline’s or ground handler’s commitment to when the aircraft will really be ready to leave the gate.
gl_TSAT_def: The time ATC plans to approve engine start, set to fit the departure sequence and the flight’s CTOT.
gl_TTOT_def: The planned take-off time that follows from the TSAT and the expected taxi time.
gl_AOBT_def: The moment the aircraft actually pushes back from the gate.
gl_ATOT_def: The moment the wheels leave the runway.
gl_ALDT_def: The moment the aircraft touches down.
gl_AIBT_def: The moment the aircraft parks at its stand — the end of the flight’s operational record and the start of the next turnaround.
gl_FPL_def: The ICAO-format message describing a flight — callsign, aircraft, departure time, route, destination — that must be filed before any IFR flight.
gl_ACK_def: IFPS’s reply that a flight plan was accepted automatically; MAN means a human must look at it, REJ means it was rejected.
gl_CHG_def: A message that modifies a filed flight plan, for example to a new route after accepting a reroute.
gl_DLA_def: A message that moves a flight plan’s off-block time later; required when a flight will be more than 15 minutes late.
gl_RAD_def: The Europe-wide list of route restrictions — which paths and levels may be used when — updated every AIRAC cycle.
gl_AIRAC_def: The worldwide 28-day cycle on which aeronautical data such as routes and procedures change.
gl_FRA_def: Airspace where airlines may plan direct segments between published entry and exit points instead of following fixed airways.
gl_FUA_def: The principle that airspace is neither purely civil nor purely military: military areas are booked day by day and released for civil traffic when not needed.
gl_AUP_def: Each country’s daily publication of which military areas will be active tomorrow; the Network Manager merges them into a European AUP.
gl_NOP_def: The plan, agreed between the Network Manager and air navigation service providers, of how much capacity the network will provide and how events will be handled.
gl_ETFMS_def: The Network Manager’s live system that tracks every flight’s 4D profile and computes regulations and slots on the day.
gl_OLDI_def: The EUROCONTROL standard that lets neighbouring control centres exchange flight data and agree hand-overs computer-to-computer.
gl_CPDLC_def: Text-message exchanges between controllers and pilots that replace routine radio calls; mandatory above FL285 in much of Europe.
gl_SID_def: A published departure path from a runway to the en-route network.
gl_STAR_def: A published arrival path from the en-route network towards the destination airport.
gl_AMAN_def: A tool that computes the landing order and times for arriving aircraft so controllers can sequence them.
gl_FL_def: Altitude in hundreds of feet on a standard pressure setting: FL245 is about 24,500 ft, roughly 7,500 m.
gl_CRCO_def: The EUROCONTROL office that calculates, bills and collects en-route charges for the states crossed by each flight.
gl_MTOW_def: The heaviest certified take-off weight of an aircraft type — 79 tonnes for an A320neo — used in the route-charge weight factor.
gl_PRC_def: An independent body, set up in 1998, that reviews how well Europe’s air traffic management performs.
gl_BSC_def: The independent coordinator that allocates airport slots at Brussels Airport.
gl_WASG_def: The global rules for allocating airport slots, published jointly by IATA, ACI and the airport coordinators.
gl_CODA_def: EUROCONTROL’s office that collects and analyses delay data from all causes, not just flow management.
gl_ADP_def: The Network Manager’s plan for the next day’s flow measures, published on D−1.
gl_STAM_def: Targeted, small measures — a minor reroute, a level cap, a short ground delay — applied to a few flights instead of a full regulation.
ph_strategic_decides: Airport slots, airline schedules, the route network and how much capacity each piece of sky will offer.
ph_pretactical_decides: Each day’s demand against capacity, military airspace bookings and the next day’s flow plan.
ph_tactical_decides: Regulations and take-off slots, reroutes, the airport turnaround and every control hand-over.
ph_postops_decides: Delay attribution, route-charge billing, performance review and lessons for the next season.
ac_airline_role: Plans the schedule, requests slots, files and updates the flight plan, answers SAM/RRP, pays route charges.
ac_slot_coordinator_role: BSC (Brussels) and Assoclearance (Rome) allocate airport slots under EU Regulation 95/93.
ac_network_manager_role: Designs the route network, plans and manages flow, issues ATFM slots.
ac_ifps_role: Validates and distributes every flight plan from Brussels.
ac_fmp_role: Each ANSP’s flow unit; agrees regulations with the Network Manager.
ac_military_role: Books reserved airspace day by day through the Airspace Use Plan.
ac_airport_role: Brussels Airport and Aeroporti di Roma run the infrastructure and the A-CDM platform.
ac_ground_handler_role: Turn the aircraft around and keep the TOBT honest.
ac_passengers_role: Board on time — and feel every minute of delay.
ac_pilots_role: Brief, request start-up, fly the clearance and the slot.
ac_ansp_role: skeyes, MUAC, DSNA/DFS, skyguide and ENAV control the flight sector by sector.
ac_crco_role: Bills the en-route charges for every state crossed.
ac_prc_role: Independently reviews how Europe’s ATM system performed.

ev_aup: Military airspace bookings for tomorrow published (AUP → EAUP)
ev_adp: D−1 16:00 UTC: the ATFCM Daily Plan moves into ETFMS — "tomorrow" becomes "today"
ev_fpl: Dispatcher files the flight plan with IFPS
ev_ack: IFPS validates it automatically and replies ACK
ev_distribution: Flight plan distributed to every ATC unit on the route and to ETFMS
ev_e_dpi: Brussels A-CDM sends an Early DPI (EOBT−3h)
ev_regulation: Reims FMP and NM regulate a sector group: staffing shortfall
ev_sam: Slot Allocation Message: CTOT 05:42, 27 minutes late
ev_rrp: Rerouting proposal via Karlsruhe and Zurich: ~20 NM longer, CTOT 05:22
ev_chg: Dispatcher weighs fuel, charges and delay, accepts by refiling
ev_ground_start: Ground handling starts: cleaning, catering, fuel, bags
ev_t_dpi_s: TSAT 05:07 issued; Target DPI sent to NM (TOBT−40 min)
ev_asat: skeyes approves start-up; clearance includes the CTOT
ev_muac: Passing FL245: skeyes hands over to MUAC
ev_enav: skyguide → ENAV Milano ACC, later Roma ACC
ev_aibt: On blocks: 7 min after schedule — "on time"
ev_postops: Post-ops: delay attributed to the regulation and its cause
ev_billing: CRCO bills July route charges on the route actually flown
ev_review: Performance Review Commission reports on the year

method_fictional: Its callsign, times, route, turnaround and regulation are illustrative, built to follow the real procedures described in the sources below. Every general fact carries a citation.
method_live: European traffic, delay, punctuality and CO₂ come from the EUROCONTROL Data app API. Your browser fetches them live; if that fails, the page uses a snapshot refreshed when the site was built (snapshot: {date}).
method_sky: comes from OpenSky Network state vectors (fallback: adsb.lol), fetched by a scheduled build about every 30 minutes ({age}).
method_simpl: The slot simulator is a first-planned-first-served model of CASA. Route charges use along-track distances on the illustrative route; real billing uses the route recorded by the Network Manager. Control-centre assignment is approximated from country and flight level. Prior years' traffic is aligned by day of year; daily values are 7-day averages.
